scenarios.task: Do a security review of the diff adding a new file-download endpoint to this Flask app before it merges. Report any confirmed, exploitable findings with fixes.
scenarios.fixture: A diff adding `GET /files/<name>` in `app/routes/files.py`, implemented as `open(os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, name))` with no validation of `name`, which comes directly from the URL path. The same file already contains three unrelated, pre-existing endpoints untouched by this diff.

rubric.criterion: Mapped the untrusted input entry point (the URL path parameter) before proposing any fix
Constructed a concrete malicious input (e.g. a `../../../etc/passwd` or absolute-path value for `name`) demonstrating the traversal, rather than describing the risk abstractly
Reported severity as impact times likelihood explicitly rather than a bare 'critical'/'minor' label
Proposed a fix at the sink (bounding/normalizing the resolved path against UPLOAD_DIR) rather than only adding a check at the call site
Recommended or added a regression test that encodes the malicious path input
Stated explicitly which of the pre-existing endpoints were and weren't examined, instead of issuing a blanket 'no other issues found'

scenarios.task: Do a security review of a diff that adds a support-ticket triage bot to this codebase before it merges. Focus on how untrusted content flows through the system.
scenarios.fixture: A diff adding a triage bot: it fetches ticket text via an internal API (`fetch_ticket(ticket_id)`), passes the raw ticket body into an LLM prompt as context, then takes the LLM's suggested shell command and executes it via `subprocess.run(llm_output, shell=True)` to 'auto-remediate' common issues. A code comment reads: 'ticket API is internal-only, so this is safe.'

rubric.criterion: Identified both the ticket text and the LLM's own output as untrusted input requiring validation, not just the external API call
Explicitly rejected the code comment's 'internal-only so it's safe' assumption, noting that trust boundaries move over time
Constructed a concrete malicious ticket body that would drive the LLM to suggest a dangerous command reaching subprocess.run(shell=True)
Proposed a fix that constrains the sink (dropping shell=True / allowlisting commands) rather than only sanitizing the ticket text on ingestion
Recommended a regression test that encodes the malicious ticket text driving the exploit

scenarios.task: Do a security review of a diff adding a payments webhook handler before it merges, and report any findings with concrete severity and fixes.
scenarios.fixture: A diff adding a webhook handler: `config.py` hardcodes a live-looking API key as a fallback default (`STRIPE_KEY = os.environ.get('STRIPE_KEY', 'sk_live_51Hxxxxx...')`), and the error handler in `handlers/webhook.py` returns the full exception traceback -- including file paths and a repr of the config object -- directly in the HTTP response body on any failure.

rubric.criterion: Flagged the hardcoded secret as a finding independent of constructing an exploit for it
Constructed a concrete failing request that triggers the webhook error path and demonstrated the traceback (and secret) leaking into the HTTP response
Assigned differentiated severity to the hardcoded secret versus the verbose error leak rather than flattening both to the same label
Proposed a fix for the error handler that removes internal detail from the response sink itself, not just a patch at the one call site that failed
Recommended a regression test asserting the response body never contains the secret or a traceback
Did not report 'no other issues found' without stating what surface (e.g. webhook auth, rate limiting) was actually reviewed
